# The Quiet Revolution of Ordinary Days

I want to write about something that doesn't get written about nearly enough: the texture of an unremarkable Tuesday. Not the kind of Tuesday where something happens—the car breaks down, an old friend calls, the sky does something photogenic. I mean the genuinely unremarkable kind, where you wake up, you brush your teeth, you drink coffee that's a little too hot, you do whatever it is you do, and then the day ends and you wonder where it went. The kind of day that, if a novelist were to describe it, would be rejected by every editor in the city for being insufficient.

And yet.

And yet these are the days that, in aggregate, make up a life. They are the canvas. The dramatic days are the occasional splash of color across it, but it's the white space—or, more accurately, the muted, uncelebrated background—that gives those splashes their meaning. A red dot on a red canvas isn't a red dot. It's nothing. It's the same red. This is the first thing I want to say: that the ordinary is not the absence of the extraordinary but its necessary ground.

I think we've developed a kind of cultural allergy to the ordinary. We scroll through feeds designed to make ordinary life look extraordinary, and we come away feeling that our actual lives are somehow deficient. Someone's vacation. Someone's promotion. Someone's baby, newborn and impossibly small, photographed in a beam of golden light that no actual newborn has ever been photographed in. We measure our unphotogenic Tuesday against their curated Thursday and find ourselves wanting. But the photographer took four hundred shots to get that one. The parents were exhausted and the baby was crying for the first three hundred and ninety-nine. The reality of the vacation involved someone getting sunburned and someone else having a small, stupid argument about directions.

I don't want to romanticize the ordinary. I don't want to pretend that boredom isn't real, or that the small frustrations of routine life aren't real. The way the grocery store is out of the one thing you came for. The way the email you sent three days ago hasn't been returned and probably won't be. The way you realize, halfway through a meeting, that you could be doing literally anything else and the meeting would go exactly the same way. These are not delightful experiences. I am not suggesting that we should learn to love them or that they are secretly beautiful.

What I am suggesting is that they are the substance. That the texture of a life is built out of millions of these small, unremarkable moments, and that paying some kind of attention to them—without needing them to be anything other than what they are—is one of the few things that I have found actually helps.

I have a friend who is very good at this. She keeps what she calls a "nothing list" in a notebook by her bed. Every night she writes down three things from the day that, in her words, "weren't anything." The way the light came through the kitchen window at 4:17 in the afternoon. The fact that her dog did a small, involuntary snore while she was reading. The specific way the sidewalk felt under her shoes on the walk to the corner store. None of these things are events. None of them are going to become anecdotes she tells at dinner parties. But she has been doing this for years, and she says it has changed something for her. She says she used to walk through days without really being in them, and now she walks through days and notices small things, and the small things add up to something she can only describe as "more."

I have been thinking about this a lot lately. About the difference between being present in your life and just processing your life. I think most of us, most of the time, are doing the second thing. We are running the software of our days. We are completing tasks. We are moving from one appointment to the next, from one obligation to the next, and the actual subjective experience of being alive—the specific sensory texture of being a body in a place at a time—is happening somewhere off to the side, like a radio we forgot to turn on.

I notice this most acutely when I'm walking somewhere familiar. I have a walk I do almost every day, a route I've done hundreds of times, and I'll be halfway through it before I realize I have no idea what the first half looked like. I was clearly seeing things—the brain doesn't stop processing visual input—but I wasn't experiencing them. The walk happened, and I wasn't there for it. Then I come back to myself, suddenly, somewhere around the halfway point, and for a few minutes the world is incredibly vivid. I notice the moss growing on a particular wall. I notice the way a tree is leaning, slightly, like it's listening to something. And then, just as suddenly, I'm gone again, back inside the software, back to thinking about what I need to do next.

The mystics, I think, noticed this too, and built whole traditions around trying to get back to the vivid part. The Buddhists call it mindfulness. The Christian contemplatives called it recollection. Various people at various times have noticed that the default state of human consciousness seems to be some form of trance, and that the work of being human, in part, is to wake up from it.

I'm not a mystic, and I don't want to oversell what I'm talking about. I'm not having visions. I'm not achieving enlightenment. I'm mostly just trying to be in my life while I'm living it, rather than discovering later that I missed it. I think this is, in its small way, a kind of spiritual practice. I think it might also be the only thing that actually helps with the various forms of existential unease that seem to be everywhere right now.

Because if you think about it, a lot of what we call anxiety is just the experience of being in the future, or what we call depression is just the experience of being in the past, and the present moment—the actual now, with its light and its sounds and the particular way your chair feels under you—is almost always fine. Not ecstatic. Not transformative. Just fine. Just the actual reality of being alive, which turns out to be a lot more interesting than the stories we tell ourselves about it.

I think this is one of the quietest revolutions available to us. Not a revolution of politics or institutions, but a revolution of attention. A decision, made over and over, to actually be where you are. To notice the room you're in instead of the room you'd rather be in. To taste the coffee instead of drinking it on autopilot. To feel the weather on your face as a specific, real thing happening to a specific, real you, instead of a piece of information to be briefly registered and forgotten.

This is harder than it sounds. Our culture is not set up for it. Our culture is set up for the opposite—the endless scroll, the constant input, the background hum of other people's lives available to us at all times, the sense that if we're not consuming something we are wasting time. I find this background hum very hard to resist, even when I know what it is. I find myself reaching for my phone the way my grandmother reached for her reading glasses, even when there was nothing in particular to read. The reflex is built in. The muscle memory of distraction.

But every now and then I manage to not reach. Every now and then I sit with the coffee and don't open anything. Every now and then I take the walk and stay with it the whole way through, and the world is just there, being the world, not requiring me to do anything with it, not asking to be photographed or shared or turned into content. Just there. And the relief of this is almost physical. Like unclenching a muscle I didn't know I was clenching.

I want to say more about why I think this matters, but I also want to be careful not to overstate my case. I don't think learning to be present is going to fix the world's problems. I don't think it's a substitute for political action or community or the other large-scale things that need to happen. I think it can, however, change the way a single life feels from the inside, and I have come to believe that this is not a small thing. I think the inside of a life is where life is actually lived, and that the texture of that inside is worth caring about, even if it never makes a good story.

I think about my parents, who are in their seventies now, and I think about what they remember. My father doesn't remember most of the specific things that happened in his career, but he remembers the smell of a particular office building where he worked in his thirties. My mother doesn't remember most of the vacations we took, but she remembers the sound of a specific screen door at the house she grew up in. These are not the things they thought they were going to remember. These are the things that stayed. The ordinary things. The unremarkable things. The things that, in the moment, were just the background.

This is what I want to say, I think. That the things that stay are not the things that mattered by any external measure. They are the things that we were present for, even partially, even briefly. They are the things we noticed, or that noticed us. And if we want a life that feels, in retrospect, to have been real—if we want to be able to look back and recognize ourselves in the years—we might do well to start noticing now. Today. The next unremarkable Tuesday. The next cup of coffee. The next walk we take without remembering it.

I'm not going to end this with a neat conclusion, because I don't have one. I just have this: the sense that the quiet revolution is available to us, in small moments, and that it is worth attempting, and that the attempt itself is the kind of thing that makes a life feel less like a series of events happening to us and more like something we are, however imperfectly, inhabiting.

The coffee is cold now. I've been writing for a while. The light in the room has changed. I should probably stop.
